meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I used to think that the brain was the most important organ in my body, but then I thought: look who's telling me that'?
meta.ogDescription: Not George Carlin. The joke is Emo Philips's, from a 1987 HBO special. The wording quoted today comes from Richard Saul Wurman's 1992 paraphrase of him.

answer.label: Not George Carlin — actually Emo Philips
answer.sourceLine: The joke is Emo Philips’s. Quote Investigator’s earliest match ↗ is a comedy special starring Philips broadcast in 1987 on HBO, where he said “I used to think that the human brain was the most fascinating part of the body. Then I realized, whoa, ‘look what’s telling me that’.” The smoother “most important organ” wording quoted today is not what Philips is recorded as saying in 1987 — it first appears as an acknowledged paraphrase in Richard Saul Wurman’s 1992 book Follow the Yellow Brick Road, though Quote Investigator adds that variant phrasings proliferated and that Philips may have told the joke more than one way. Quote Investigator calls the Carlin linkage unsupported, and the line also fails the test Carlin set for himself ↗ — albums, books, HBO specials or his website.

source.excerpt: I used to think that the human brain was the most fascinating part of the body. Then I realized, whoa, ‘look what’s telling me that’.
trail: 1987. Quote Investigator’s earliest located match ↗ is a comedy special starring Emo Philips broadcast on the cable channel HBO: “I used to think that the human brain was the most fascinating part of the body. Then I realized, whoa, ‘look what’s telling me that’.” The Indianapolis News of 26 March 1987 reported it the same season.

1992. Richard Saul Wurman prints the “most important organ” wording on page 124 of Follow the Yellow Brick Road and marks it “Paraphrased from comedian Emo Phillips” — as documented by Quote Investigator ↗. The book is catalogued as Bantam Books, 1992 ↗.

2017. Daniel C. Dennett prints a close variant — “For years and years and years, I thought my brain was the most important organ of my body, until one day I thought, hmm. Look who’s telling me that!” — the form Wurman himself used in a 2010 keynote, introducing it as “one of my favorite George Carlin one-liners.” Quote Investigator records that instance and calls the Carlin linkage unsupported ↗; it is the earliest printed Carlin credit the investigation located. Dennett’s book itself is From Bacteria to Bach and Back (W. W. Norton, 2017) ↗.

The standing caveat. Carlin attracted so much orphaned material that Wikipedia keeps an “Internet hoaxes” section on him ↗, recording his own rule that nothing on the internet is his unless it came from his albums, books, HBO specials or his website. This line meets none of those tests.
source.excerptNote: Emo Philips’s delivery in the 1987 HBO special, as transcribed by Quote Investigator. The version that circulates today — “the most important organ in my body, but then I thought: look who’s telling me that” — is Wurman’s 1992 paraphrase, which reads “my brain” where the popular form has “the brain.”

source.rightsNote: Both layers of this quotation are modern and protected. The sentence as quoted was published in Richard Saul Wurman’s Follow the Yellow Brick Road (Bantam Books, 1992), and the joke it paraphrases was performed by Emo Philips in a 1987 HBO special — each far later than the 1931 United States public-domain threshold. Nothing here is public domain; brief quotation for commentary and attribution purposes only.

author.name: Emo Philips
author.heading: The comedian who actually built the joke
author.bio: Born Philip Soltanec in Chicago on 7 February 1956, Emo Philips has performed stand-up since 1976 in a fidgety, falsetto-voiced persona built almost entirely out of paraprosdokians — sentences whose second half ambushes the first. His 1985 album E=mo² won the New Music Award for best comedy album, and a joke of his was voted the funniest religious joke ever in a 2005 online poll. The brain line is a textbook Philips construction: a straight-faced compliment that turns and eats itself.

misattribution.heading: Two things are wrong here at once
misattribution.intro: This line is misattributed twice over: the wrong comedian gets the credit, and the wording is not the right comedian’s either.

items.why: The earliest printed Carlin credit located by Quote Investigator is Daniel C. Dennett’s 2017 book From Bacteria to Bach and Back: The Evolution of Minds (W. W. Norton), which introduces the quip as “one of my favorite George Carlin one-liners.” Quote Investigator states the linkage to Carlin is currently unsupported ↗. Separately, the line fails the test Carlin set for himself, recorded on Wikipedia ↗: nothing is his unless it came from his albums, books, HBO specials or his website.

The “most important organ” phrasing is the form Richard Saul Wurman printed on page 124 of Follow the Yellow Brick Road (Bantam Books, 1992) — as “my brain”, where the circulating version has “the brain” — and expressly labelled there “Paraphrased from comedian Emo Phillips.” Quote Investigator reproduces both the wording and the credit line ↗. Philips’s recorded 1987 delivery said “the most fascinating part of the body” — though Quote Investigator cautions that variant phrasings proliferated and that Philips may have presented the quip in more than one way.

A third form — “I used to think that the brain was the most wonderful organ in my body. Then I realized who was telling me this” — is the one most quote sites carry. Quote Investigator’s chronology records it in the Albuquerque Journal in 1999 ↗, twelve years after the joke was first documented — credited there to Emo Phillips. This one is a rewording, not a misattribution.

misattribution.truthLine: The joke belongs to Emo Philips, whose 1987 HBO comedy special is the earliest match Quote Investigator located ↗; the sentence people quote is a 1992 book’s paraphrase of him; and George Carlin has nothing to do with either.

context.heading: How a comedian’s line became a philosopher’s Carlin quote
lead: Philips’s original is rougher and funnier than the version that circulates: he called the brain “the most fascinating part of the body,” then broke off with “whoa” before the turn. Contemporary press coverage in March 1987 already reported it, and Quote Investigator quotes the Indianapolis News of 26 March 1987 ↗ rendering the punchline as “Look who’s telling me that.”

The polish came later, and from outside comedy. Richard Saul Wurman — the information architect who had co-founded the TED conference in 1984 — retold the joke in his 1992 book Follow the Yellow Brick Road, tidying “most fascinating part of the body” into “most important organ in my body” and, to his credit, printing “Paraphrased from comedian Emo Phillips” alongside it. Quote Investigator is careful to leave the door open here — variant phrasings proliferated, and Philips may have told the joke more than one way — but Wurman’s is the earliest print appearance of this form, and it is the version the internet inherited. What it did not inherit was the credit line.
detailsBody: George Carlin is one of the internet’s most reliable magnets for orphaned material. Wikipedia’s article on him carries a dedicated “Internet hoaxes” section ↗ covering joke lists and rants pinned on him, and records Carlin’s own standing rule: nothing on the internet is his unless it came from his albums, books, HBO specials or his website.

In this case the false credit did not stay on social media. In 2017 the philosopher Daniel C. Dennett printed the Wurman-style wording in From Bacteria to Bach and Back: The Evolution of Minds and introduced it as one of his favourite George Carlin one-liners — which is how an unsourced attribution acquires the authority of a hardback from W. W. Norton. Quote Investigator flags that credit as unsupported ↗.
context.pull: The wording everyone quotes is not the comedian’s. It is a 1992 book’s tidy-up of him — with the attribution left behind.
